analysis.one_liner: Traded federal welfare and food programs for a full federal takeover of Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The Republican welfare-and-Medicaid swap, introduced by Senator Kassebaum with four cosponsors, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the four big federal safety-net programs for poor families — cash aid (AFDC), job training, WIC food aid for mothers and infants, and food stamps — after fiscal 1995, and handed the job of helping those families to the states. States would pay for it with money they currently send Washington for Medicaid, getting a roughly equal federal check back. The twist: starting in fiscal 2000, the federal government would take over Medicaid entirely, paying the whole bill and freeing states of it.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments gain the most: they would stop paying their share of Medicaid after 2000 and would receive federal block payments (growing only with inflation) to run their own low-income assistance programs. Poor families would keep their current benefits for five years under a maintenance-of-effort requirement, and after 2000 everyone on Medicaid would be covered by a single federal program rather than 50 different state versions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State governments, and Medicaid recipients after 2000

how_it_helps.text: State governments would be relieved of all financial and administrative responsibility for Medicaid beginning October 1, 2000, with the federal government paying all program costs [S2][S3].

States would receive guaranteed federal payments each year from 1996 through 2000, equal to what the federal government had been spending on AFDC, food stamps, WIC, and JOBS in that state, adjusted upward only for inflation [S3].

States would be required to maintain their existing level of assistance to low-income families — the prior year's spending plus inflation plus estimated caseload growth — or lose the federal payments, protecting current beneficiaries for five years [S3].
A single national Medicaid program run by the federal government after 2000 would replace a patchwork of state eligibility rules and benefit levels [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would take on the entire cost of Medicaid after 2000, a large open-ended obligation. Low-income families would carry the long-term risk: the block funding for welfare and food assistance grows only with inflation, so in a recession or a spike in unemployment, money would not follow need. After 2000, states could also cut Medicaid eligibility as long as total spending stayed under a cap [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and long-term aid recipients

drawbacks.text: The block grant grows only with the consumer price index, not with caseload: in a recession, more families would seek aid but funding would not rise, meaning either lower benefits per family or state tax increases [S3].
During 1998-2000 states could change Medicaid eligibility rules as long as aggregate spending did not exceed what the old plan would have cost, allowing states to narrow who qualifies [S3].

Ending AFDC and food stamps as federal entitlements removes the guarantee that eligible families nationally receive help, and replaces nationally uniform rules with 50 separate state programs of varying generosity [S2].
The bill's funding formula and the state maintenance-of-effort requirement both expire after fiscal 2000, leaving the future of state welfare programs undefined and uncertain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a genuine two-way trade, not a disguised cut: states got Medicaid off their books permanently, and in exchange had to keep helping poor families at current levels for five years. The federal takeover of Medicaid was the strongest part of the deal for low-income households, guaranteeing uniform coverage nationwide. The weak part was the welfare side: converting guaranteed federal entitlements into a block grant that grows only with inflation is risky in exactly the times aid is most needed, and the design simply runs out after 2000. A fair bill, but one whose long-term protections were thinner than what it replaced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1994 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas introduced the bill on March 7, 1994, with four Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S1][S5].
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's only recorded actions after referral were the sponsor's introductory remarks [S5].
The bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died, the existing federal entitlements — AFDC, food stamps, and WIC, with national eligibility standards and funding that rises with need — continued unchanged, and state governments never got the Medicaid relief they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal welfare entitlements; state governments lost out

for.name: Sen. Nancy Landon Kassebaum
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. Bob Bennett, Hank Brown, Larry Craig, and John Danforth

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Daniel Patrick Moynihan)
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration during the 18 months before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure partisanship; all five sponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: States would shed their share of Medicaid costs permanently after 2000 and receive federal block payments for welfare instead — the clearest winners in the trade. The benefit to their residents was real but hedged, since state aid levels would no longer be nationally guaranteed.

industries.industry: Health care providers treating Medicaid patients (hospitals, nursing homes, physicians)
industries.note: The bill keeps Medicaid flowing — first through state plans, then through a fully federal program after 2000 — so provider revenue streams continue and become federally guaranteed. Recipients and providers both keep the program, under one national payer.

industries.industry: Low-income families receiving AFDC, food stamps, and WIC
industries.note: Current benefits would be maintained for five years by a hard maintenance-of-effort requirement, but after 2000 the guarantee lapses and funding grows only with inflation, not with need.
